about: POL2 is the International Relations paper an option for first-year HSPS students (POLIS advises those planning the Politics and International Relations track to take it with POL1) and is taken by all History and Politics students. It introduces modern international politics and the discipline of IR through a global, historical approach starting around 1500, running from early encounters and state formation through IR theory, 20th-century challenges to Anglo-American order and the Cold War, to global governance, decolonisation, human rights, the global economy and the current crisis of the liberal international order. The latest openable paper guide (2024-25) describes 25 lectures across Michaelmas and Lent with supervisions, and a three-hour in-person exam in which students answer 2 of 8 questions, each worth half the mark. The HSPS site confirms that all Part I exams in 2026-27 are invigilated and in person; check the current guide on Moodle for any changes.
topics: First encounters and early modern global orders (c.1500–1800)
Europe, the sovereign state and the Westphalian myth
Nations and states in the Americas; the Great Divergence and European imperialism
IR theory: realism, liberal internationalism and constructivism
Challenges to Pax Anglo-America: Germany, the USSR, Japan and Britain's global role
The Cold War, nuclear weapons and the end of the Cold War
Global governance, decolonisation and post-colonial intervention
Human rights, gender and regulating the use of force
Power in the global economy and governing the global commons
The crisis of the liberal international order: the West, Russia and China

notes.h: First encounters and early modern global orders
notes.body:
POL2 opens in c.1500, not in 1945 or 1648. The point is to unsettle the standard story that a European "international society" grew up on its own and then spread outwards. In the early modern world several international orders existed side by side, and Europeans were often weak newcomers in them.

The traditional (Eurocentric) story
- Hedley Bull and Adam Watson, The Expansion of International Society (1984): a European society of sovereign states expanded until it covered the globe.
- Gerrit Gong, The Standard of 'Civilization' in International Society (1984): non-Europeans were admitted to the club only once they met European legal and political standards.
- The critique: this treats non-European polities as passive. It reads later 19th-century European dominance back into a period when it did not exist.

East Asia: Europeans as supplicants
- Ming and then Qing China ran relations through a hierarchical tributary order. The Portuguese reached China in 1513, and later Europeans had to fit into Chinese rules about trade and ritual. Yongjin Zhang describes Europeans as "supplicants" in the Chinese imperium (1513–1793).
- The Macartney embassy of 1793 is the classic end-point. The Qianlong emperor turned down British requests for wider trade and a permanent embassy.
- Japan: the Tokugawa shogunate (from 1603) tightly controlled foreign contact. Adam Clulow, The Company and the Shogun (2014), shows that the Dutch East India Company (VOC, founded 1602) acted like a sovereign power elsewhere in Asia. In Japan, by contrast, it had to recast itself as a loyal subordinate of the shogun. From 1641 the Dutch were confined to the artificial island of Dejima at Nagasaki.

The Americas: conquest and mutual misreading
- The Spanish conquered the Mexica (Aztec) empire in 1519–21 and the Inca from 1532. Here encounter did lead to conquest, settler colonisation and demographic catastrophe, mostly from disease.
- James Lockhart, a historian of the Nahuas, stresses that indigenous structures survived after the conquest. His idea of "double mistaken identity" is that each side assumed a given form or concept worked as it did in its own tradition, so Nahua practices could carry on under Spanish-looking forms. Conquest was real, but it was not simply Europeans imposing their will on a blank slate.

Other powers
- The Ottoman Empire (which took Constantinople in 1453), Safavid Iran and Mughal India (from 1526) were major land empires. Europeans dealt with them on the empires' own terms.
- Suzuki, Zhang and Quirk (eds), International Orders in the Early Modern World (2014), argue for plural, overlapping orders, not one expanding European system.

Was early modern European expansion "colonial"?
- In the Americas, largely yes: territorial conquest, settlement, coerced labour and the Atlantic slave trade.
- In much of Asia and Africa before c.1800, mostly not: there were trading posts, chartered companies and coastal forts that depended on local rulers.
- The answer therefore depends on region and date. The best essays avoid one blanket answer.

Exam tips: Use a comparison across at least two regions (e.g. Japan and Mexico) to show that "encounter" produced very different outcomes. Link to the theory lectures: which theory can explain hierarchical, non-Westphalian orders such as the Chinese tributary system?

notes.h: The sovereign state and the Westphalian myth
notes.body:
IR textbooks often date the modern states system to the Peace of Westphalia (1648). POL2 asks two questions: why did the sovereign territorial state win out in Europe, and does Westphalia deserve its iconic status?

Key definitions
- Sovereignty: supreme authority within a territory (internal) and independence from outside authority (external). Theorised by Jean Bodin, Les Six Livres de la République (1576), and Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651).
- "Westphalian sovereignty" (Stephen Krasner, Sovereignty: Organized Hypocrisy, 1999): outside actors are excluded from a state's domestic authority structures. Krasner argues that states routinely breach this norm, so it is "organised hypocrisy".

Why the sovereign state? Explanations
- War-making (Charles Tilly): "War made the state, and the state made war" (1975). In Coercion, Capital, and European States, AD 990–1990 (1990), rulers who could extract resources to fight survived. Tilly identifies coercion-intensive, capital-intensive and "capitalised coercion" paths.
- Institutional selection (Hendrik Spruyt, The Sovereign State and Its Competitors, 1994): after the late-medieval economic revival, three kinds of unit competed: sovereign territorial states, city-leagues (e.g. the Hanseatic League) and city-states (e.g. in Italy). Territorial states won not just through war. They were better at standardising coinage, weights and law, at curbing free-riding, and at making credible commitments to other actors. Rulers also preferred to deal with, and recognise, units like themselves.
- Concepts and words: a 2018 International Studies Review forum (Costa Lopez et al.) warns that early modern actors lacked our vocabulary of "sovereignty". Historians must ask whether the concept existed before the word.

Westphalia (1648): the conventional story
- The treaties of Münster and Osnabrück ended the Thirty Years' War (1618–48). At Münster, Spain also recognised Dutch independence, ending the Eighty Years' War.
- Textbook claims: Westphalia created a system of sovereign, legally equal states, established non-intervention and ended religious wars.

The "Westphalian myth" critique
- Andreas Osiander, "Sovereignty, International Relations, and the Westphalian Myth" (International Organization, 2001): the treaties were mainly about the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire and the rights of its estates. They did not create sovereignty. The Empire survived until 1806, and France and Sweden became guarantors with a right to involve themselves in imperial affairs, which is the opposite of non-intervention.
- On religion, the settlement modified the Peace of Augsburg (1555, cuius regio, eius religio). It used 1624 as a "normative year" to protect existing religious rights, so it limited what rulers could do, not just freed them.
- Stéphane Beaulac (2000) traces the "Westphalian legal orthodoxy" to later writers, notably Vattel's Law of Nations (1758) and 19th-century international lawyers.

Does Westphalia still matter?
- As a myth, yes. It shapes how IR dates "modernity", how theorists define the system (anarchy among like units) and how states talk. China and Russia often invoke "Westphalian" non-interference, and the EU is described as "post-Westphalian".
- Critics say the myth is Eurocentric. It also hides the persistence of empire, hierarchy and composite monarchies long after 1648.

Exam tips: A past question asked "Does Westphalia matter for contemporary international politics?" Separate the event (what the treaties did) from the idea (what later writers made of it). Bring in Spruyt or Tilly to explain state formation independently of 1648.

notes.h: Nations and states in the Americas; the Great Divergence and imperialism
notes.body:
This part of the paper asks how new states were made outside Europe, and why Europe came to dominate much of the world in the 19th century.

State and nation-building in the Americas
- Waves of independence: the United States (declared 1776, recognised 1783), Haiti (1804, the first state founded by formerly enslaved people after the revolution of 1791–1804), Spanish America (c.1808–1820s) and Brazil (1822, under a Portuguese prince, Pedro I).
- Jaime Rodríguez, "The Emancipation of America" (American Historical Review, 2000): Spanish American independence was less an anticolonial nationalist revolt than the break-up of a transatlantic Spanish Monarchy. The trigger was Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808. The Cádiz Constitution of 1812 brought American representatives into a common political community before the empire fragmented.
- Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983), controversially saw American "creole pioneers" as early nationalists. Rodríguez's account challenges any simple story of pre-existing nations seeking states.
- Miguel Centeno, Blood and Debt (2002): Latin America mostly had "limited wars". With few total interstate wars, states did not need to build Tilly-style tax-and-army machines. They relied on customs revenues and foreign loans, which left them institutionally weaker. Exceptions such as the Paraguayan War (1864–70) and the War of the Pacific (1879–84) test the argument.
- Violence was central. Independence wars, civil wars and campaigns against indigenous peoples (e.g. US Indian removal after 1830; Argentina's "Conquest of the Desert", late 1870s–1880s) shaped borders and national identities.
- The Monroe Doctrine (1823) declared the Americas closed to new European colonisation.

The Great Divergence
- Why did north-west Europe pull ahead economically from c.1800?
- Kenneth Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000), is the leading text of the "California School". The Yangzi Delta and England were broadly comparable until the late 18th century. Britain diverged because of conveniently located coal and the resources of the New World colonies ("ghost acres"), which eased land constraints.
- Critics such as Peer Vries (2010) ask whether divergence began earlier. They stress the role of states, institutions, fiscal capacity and mercantilist policy. Older explanations stress institutions, culture or the "military revolution" in European warfare.
- For IR the point is that material power became radically unequal in the 19th century, making global European dominance possible.

European imperialism and the Scramble for Africa
- The Berlin Conference (1884–85) set rules for European claims in Africa. By 1914 almost all of the continent was under European rule, Ethiopia and Liberia being the main exceptions.
- Economic explanations: J.A. Hobson, Imperialism: A Study (1902), on surplus capital and underconsumption; V.I. Lenin, Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1917).
- "Informal empire": Gallagher and Robinson, "The Imperialism of Free Trade" (1953). Britain preferred influence and trade to formal rule where it could.
- Status explanation: Joslyn Barnhart (Security Studies, 2016) argues that humiliated states seek territory to restore their standing. When they cannot hit back at the stronger humiliator, they seize land elsewhere. Example: France after defeat by Prussia (1870–71) took Tunisia in 1881.
- In Asia, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60) and the "unequal treaties" brought China into a Europe-centred order on unequal terms.

Exam tips: Supervision questions here include "Would there be no nations in the Americas without violence?" and "Can empires ever be legitimate?" Combine historical cases with a theory: Barnhart is useful for showing that status (a constructivist-friendly variable) can drive territorial expansion.

Three lectures introduce the main IR theories. Exam questions often ask you to compare them or to test one against a historical case, so you need each theory's core assumptions, key texts and typical predictions.

Realism
- Classical realism: Thucydides, Machiavelli and Hobbes are claimed as forerunners. E.H. Carr, The Twenty Years' Crisis (1939), attacked interwar "utopianism" and showed that appeals to a "harmony of interests" served satisfied powers. Hans Morgenthau, Politics Among Nations (1948), rooted power politics in human nature; the "six principles of political realism", including interest "defined in terms of power", were added in the 1954 second edition.
- Michael Williams (The Realist Tradition and the Limits of International Relations, 2005; and his "Classical Realism" chapter in Dunne, Kurki and Smith, International Relations Theories) reads classical realism as an ethical tradition concerned with prudence and the limits of power, not just cynicism.
- Neorealism (structural realism): Kenneth Waltz, Theory of International Politics (1979). The international structure is defined by (1) its ordering principle, anarchy, meaning no authority above states; (2) like units performing similar functions; and (3) the distribution of capabilities. Anarchy pushes states to self-help and balancing. Waltz thought bipolarity more stable than multipolarity.
- Offensive realism: John Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001). States maximise relative power, ideally seeking regional hegemony.
- Security dilemma: John Herz (1950) and Robert Jervis (1978). Measures one state takes for its own security make others less secure, which can produce spirals.

Liberal internationalism
- Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace (1795): republican constitutions, a federation of free states and cosmopolitan right.
- Michael Doyle, "Liberalism and World Politics" (APSR, 1986): liberal states keep a "separate peace" with one another but can be aggressive or imprudent towards non-liberal states. Doyle distinguishes liberal pacifism (Schumpeter), liberal imperialism (Machiavelli) and liberal internationalism (Kant).
- Robert Keohane, After Hegemony (1984): neoliberal institutionalism. It accepts anarchy and rational egoist states, but argues that international regimes cut transaction costs, provide information and lengthen the "shadow of the future". Cooperation can therefore continue even as US hegemony declines.
- Other strands: Keohane and Nye on complex interdependence (Power and Interdependence, 1977), and Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (1918).

Constructivism
- Alexander Wendt, "Anarchy is What States Make of It" (International Organization, 1992): anarchy has no fixed logic. Self-help results from interaction. Social Theory of International Politics (1999) describes Hobbesian (enemy), Lockean (rival) and Kantian (friend) cultures of anarchy.
- John Ruggie, "What Makes the World Hang Together?" (IO, 1998): neorealism and neoliberalism share a "neo-utilitarian" view that takes interests as given. Constructivism shows that ideas, norms and identities constitute actors and their interests.
- Norms: Finnemore and Sikkink's norm life cycle (1998); the "logic of appropriateness" versus the "logic of consequences" (March and Olsen).
- Jennifer Mitzen, "Ontological Security in World Politics" (EJIR, 2006): states seek a stable sense of self as well as physical security. They can become attached to routinised conflict, so security dilemmas can persist even when the conflict is costly.

Comparing them
- Main actors: realists say states; liberals add institutions, firms and domestic regimes; constructivists add norms and identities.
- Cooperation: realists see it as limited by relative gains; liberals see it as possible through institutions and democracy; constructivists see it as depending on shared identity.
- Change: realists point to shifts in the distribution of power; liberals to interdependence and democratisation; constructivists to new ideas and norms.

Exam tips: Avoid theory-by-numbers. Pick a case (e.g. the end of the Cold War, the rise of China, climate governance) and show what each theory explains and misses. Use theory to answer the question, not as a separate essay section.

From the late 19th century to 1945, the world order rested heavily on British and then American power: sea control, finance, trade and a large share of global territory and resources. POL2 treats Germany, the Soviet Union and Japan as three challengers, each with its own vision of order. It then asks what role Britain has had since.

Framing the challenges
- "Haves" against "have-nots": in the 1930s the revisionist powers (Germany, Italy, Japan) presented themselves as "have-not" nations, lacking land, colonies and raw materials, against satisfied status-quo powers. E.H. Carr (1939) used this language to criticise the satisfied powers' claims to speak for a universal harmony of interests.
- Race: W.E.B. Du Bois wrote in The Souls of Black Folk (1903) that "the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line". POL2 asks whether the century's great conflicts were also racial struggles over hierarchy.

Germany
- Wilhelmine Germany's Weltpolitik and naval building (Tirpitz's naval laws from 1898) challenged British sea power before 1914.
- Hitler: Mein Kampf (1925–26) set out the goal of Lebensraum in the East.
- Adam Tooze, The Wages of Destruction (2006), argues that Hitler saw the United States as the real long-term benchmark and threat. Germany needed continental scale to compete with American economic power before it became overwhelming. Rearmament strained the economy and helps explain the timing of war in 1939.
- Key dates: the invasion of the USSR (Operation Barbarossa) on 22 June 1941; Germany's declaration of war on the US on 11 December 1941.

The Soviet Union
- The Bolshevik Revolution (1917) offered an ideological alternative to liberal capitalism. Stalin's "socialism in one country" (from 1924) put building Soviet power ahead of immediate world revolution.
- Stephen Kotkin's biography of Stalin (vol. I, 2014; vol. II, 2017) stresses Stalin's geopolitical reasoning. He expected the capitalist powers to fight each other, which helps explain the Nazi–Soviet Pact (23 August 1939).
- After 1945 the Soviet challenge became the Cold War.

Japan
- After the Meiji Restoration (1868), Japan industrialised, allied with Britain (1902) and defeated Russia (1904–05).
- At the Paris Peace Conference (1919) Japan's Racial Equality Proposal failed. Naoko Shimazu, Japan, Race and Equality (1998), stresses that Japan mainly sought recognition of its own equal great-power status and equal treatment for Japanese nationals abroad, not universal racial equality.
- The Washington Naval Treaty (1922) set a 5:5:3 capital-ship ratio for the US, Britain and Japan. Many Japanese saw this as relegation.
- Japan seized Manchuria (1931), left the League of Nations (1933), went to war with China (1937) and proclaimed a "Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere" (1940).
- A US oil embargo followed Japan's move into southern Indochina in 1941. Eri Hotta, Japan 1941 (2013), shows leaders drifting into war with the US (Pearl Harbor, 7 December 1941) despite widespread doubts about victory.

"Global Britain"
- Britain went from hegemon to US junior partner. Suez (1956) exposed its limits, and Dean Acheson said in 1962 that Britain had "lost an empire and has not yet found a role". It joined the EEC in 1973.
- After the Brexit referendum (2016) and departure from the EU (31 January 2020), "Global Britain" became a slogan. The 2021 Integrated Review, "Global Britain in a Competitive Age", added an Indo-Pacific "tilt", and AUKUS followed in 2021.
- Justin Morris, "How Great is Britain?" (British Journal of Politics and International Relations, 2011), uses Hedley Bull's definition: a great power must be among the strongest militarily and must be recognised by others, and by its own leaders and people, as having special rights and duties. On this test he argues Britain's claim is stronger than often assumed, and the idea still shapes British foreign and defence policy.

Exam tips: Comparison questions are common, e.g. Japan then and China now, or the USSR then and Russia now. Set out explicit criteria (capabilities, ideology, grievances about status, the response of the dominant power) rather than listing similarities.

notes.h: The Cold War, nuclear weapons and the end of the Cold War
notes.body:
The Cold War (c.1947–1991) is the key test case for IR theory. It raises three questions: what caused it, why it stayed "cold" between the superpowers, and why it ended peacefully.

Origins and interpretations
- Orthodox view: Soviet expansionism forced a US response. George Kennan's "Long Telegram" (1946) and "X" article (1947) set out containment.
- Revisionist view: US economic expansion drove confrontation (William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy, 1959).
- Post-revisionist view: mutual misperception within a bipolar structure (e.g. John Lewis Gaddis's earlier work).
- Milestones: the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan (1947–48), NATO (April 1949), the first Soviet atomic test (August 1949), the Korean War (1950–53) and the Warsaw Pact (1955).

Was it a security dilemma?
- Robert Jervis, "Was the Cold War a Security Dilemma?" (Journal of Cold War Studies, 2001), argues that it had spiral elements but was not mainly a security dilemma. The root was a clash of social systems and visions of world order. Each side's security seemed to require changes in the other, so mutual security was hard to achieve until Soviet policy changed fundamentally.
- This matters for theory. If the conflict came from incompatible goals, reassurance alone could not end it.

Nuclear weapons
- Hiroshima (6 August 1945) and Nagasaki (9 August 1945).
- Bernard Brodie, The Absolute Weapon (1946): the chief purpose of the military would now be to avert wars, not to win them.
- Deterrence theory relies on secure second-strike capability, which produces mutual assured destruction (MAD). Thomas Schelling (The Strategy of Conflict, 1960; Arms and Influence, 1966) analysed bargaining, commitment and the "threat that leaves something to chance".
- The Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) was the closest call. It was followed by arms control: the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Non-Proliferation Treaty (signed 1968, in force 1970), SALT I and the ABM Treaty (1972), and the INF Treaty (1987).
- The "Long Peace" (Gaddis, 1986): no great-power war after 1945, partly credited to bipolarity and nuclear deterrence. Waltz even argued "more may be better" (1981) on proliferation. Nina Tannenwald points instead to a normative "nuclear taboo".
- Buzan and Hansen, The Evolution of International Security Studies (2009), show how nuclear strategy dominated Cold War security studies.
- The Global South: Odd Arne Westad, The Global Cold War (2005), stresses that the Cold War was very hot in the Third World, through proxy wars and interventions.

The end of the Cold War
- Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985, bringing glasnost, perestroika and "new thinking". The INF Treaty followed in 1987 and withdrawal from Afghanistan in 1988–89. The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, Germany reunified on 3 October 1990 and the USSR was dissolved on 26 December 1991.
- Material explanation: Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth (International Security, 2000/01) point to relative decline and the globalisation of production, which made Soviet economic isolation increasingly costly. Ideas mattered, but within these constraints.
- Ideational explanation: Gorbachev's new thinking, transnational networks of scientists and activists (Matthew Evangelista), and changed Soviet identity (Robert English, 2000).
- Method: Evangelista (2014) uses the case to show how process tracing can adjudicate between rival explanations.
- Theory's embarrassment: almost no one predicted a peaceful Soviet collapse. Francis Fukuyama's "End of History?" (1989) read it as a victory for liberal democracy.

Today: New START, the last US–Russian treaty limiting strategic nuclear forces, expired on 5 February 2026 with no replacement. Its end has revived fears of an unconstrained arms race.

Exam tips: For "Did the end of the Cold War change the fundamentals of global politics?", weigh structural change (from bipolarity to unipolarity) against continuity (nuclear deterrence, great-power rivalry returning after 2008–14).

notes.h: Global governance, decolonisation and post-colonial intervention
notes.body:
This block looks at how the order after 1945 was built, how empires broke up, and what sovereignty meant for the many new states that followed.

Origins of global governance
- G. John Ikenberry, After Victory (2001): after major wars (1815, 1919, 1945, and again after the Cold War), leading states choose how to use their power. The more they bind themselves through institutions ("strategic restraint"), the more durable and legitimate the order. The post-1945 order was the most institutionalised, or "constitutional", of these.
- Mark Mazower, Governing the World (2012), traces the idea of world governance from the Concert of Europe (1815) through 19th-century internationalism to the League of Nations (1920) and the UN. Internationalism was often entangled with great-power and imperial interests.
- Key bodies: the League's mandates system (Covenant, Article 22); the UN Charter (signed 26 June 1945, in force 24 October 1945), with a Security Council whose five permanent members hold a veto; and the Bretton Woods institutions (1944).

Decolonisation
- The UN had 51 founding members and now has 193 (South Sudan joined in 2011). Most of the growth came from decolonisation.
- Waves: India and Pakistan (1947); Indonesia (independence declared 1945, recognised 1949); Ghana (1957); the "Year of Africa" (1960), when 17 African states gained independence.
- Causes. Metropolitan: economic cost and war exhaustion. International: superpower anticolonialism and pressure at the UN. Peripheral: nationalist mobilisation and wars such as Algeria (1954–62) and Indochina (Dien Bien Phu, 1954). Normative: self-determination became a right, as in UNGA Resolution 1514 (1960), the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples. The Bandung Conference (1955) gave Afro-Asian solidarity a voice.
- Adom Getachew, Worldmaking after Empire (2019): anticolonial nationalists such as Kwame Nkrumah, Julius Nyerere, Eric Williams and Michael Manley were not just nation-building. They tried to remake the international order to end domination: self-determination as a human right at the UN, regional federations (e.g. the West Indies Federation, 1958–62) and the New International Economic Order (UNGA declaration, 1974).
- Christian Reus-Smit (International Organization, 2011): the system expanded in waves of imperial collapse, in which struggles for individual rights in imperial peripheries played a central role.

Post-colonial sovereignty and intervention
- Robert Jackson, Quasi-States (1990): post-1960 states received negative sovereignty (legal freedom from outside interference, guaranteed by international norms) without necessarily having positive sovereignty (the capacity to govern and provide public goods). Critics call this framing Eurocentric and say it understates colonial legacies and external interference.
- Martha Finnemore, The Purposes of Intervention (2003): what counts as legitimate intervention changes with norms. Forcible debt collection, accepted around 1900, became illegitimate. The circle of humans whose suffering justifies humanitarian intervention widened to include non-Europeans. Multilateral authorisation became expected.
- Cases: the Cold War interventions (Hungary 1956, Guatemala 1954, Vietnam, Afghanistan 1979); failure in Rwanda (1994); NATO's Kosovo campaign (1999), without UN Security Council authorisation; the Responsibility to Protect (ICISS report 2001, endorsed at the 2005 World Summit); and Libya (UNSC Resolution 1973, 2011), whose regime-change outcome made Russia and China more wary of R2P.
- African agency: Article 4(h) of the African Union's Constitutive Act (2000) gives the AU a right to intervene in member states in grave circumstances (war crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity).

Exam tips: For "Are post-colonial states really sovereign?", distinguish legal, empirical and economic sovereignty (Krasner's four types help). Use Getachew to show that post-colonial leaders actively fought to make sovereignty meaningful, not just received it.

notes.h: Human rights, gender and regulating the use of force
notes.body:
These lectures ask how far international norms have changed state behaviour, and whether a more just order is emerging.

International human rights
- Core texts: the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948); the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966, both in force 1976); the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998, in force 2002).
- Samuel Moyn, The Last Utopia (2010): human rights as a mass movement and moral language only broke through in the 1970s, when other utopias (socialism, anticolonial nationalism) had lost their appeal. Signs of this were Amnesty International's 1977 Nobel Prize, the Helsinki Final Act (1975) and President Carter's rights rhetoric. The 1940s declarations had little practical life.
- Kathryn Sikkink, Evidence for Hope (2017): human rights have longer and more global roots. Latin American states pushed rights in the 1940s, and the American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man was adopted months before the UDHR in 1948. Measured carefully over time, human rights work has had real effects. She is replying to pessimists such as Stephen Hopgood (The Endtimes of Human Rights, 2013).
- Mechanisms: the "boomerang" model (Keck and Sikkink, Activists Beyond Borders, 1998), in which domestic groups blocked at home enlist foreign allies to press their government; and the "spiral model" (Risse, Ropp and Sikkink, 1999).
- Enforcement is weak. The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin in March 2023, but such warrants depend on states to execute them. Human rights work mainly through socialisation, shaming and domestic courts, not coercion.

Regulating the use of force
- Legal framework: the Kellogg–Briand Pact (1928) renounced war as an instrument of policy. The UN Charter prohibits "the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state" (Article 2(4)). The exceptions are self-defence (Article 51) and Security Council action under Chapter VII (Articles 39–42).
- Tanisha Fazal, "Why States No Longer Declare War" (Security Studies, 2012): formal declarations of war have almost disappeared since 1945. The growth of codified humanitarian law (jus in bello) makes formally acknowledging a state of war costly, so states avoid triggering those obligations.
- Mark Zacher, "The Territorial Integrity Norm" (International Organization, 2001): since 1945, and especially after the mid-1970s, successful territorial conquest has become very rare. Annexations are not recognised, and borders are rarely changed by force.
- Test cases: Iraq's annexation of Kuwait (1990) was reversed. Russia annexed Crimea (2014) and then four Ukrainian regions (September 2022), which UN General Assembly resolution ES-11/4 (October 2022) condemned by 143 votes to 5. As of October 2026 the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022 continues. Direct talks in Istanbul (2025) and US-mediated trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi (January–February 2026) produced prisoner exchanges but no ceasefire or settlement. In October 2026 Moscow said it would resume US-mediated talks.

Gender in the international system
- Feminist IR asks "where are the women?" (Cynthia Enloe, Bananas, Beaches and Bases, 1989). J. Ann Tickner (1988; Gender in International Relations, 1992) argued that realism's core concepts reflect masculine assumptions.
- Ann Towns, "The Status of Women as a Standard of 'Civilization'" (EJIR, 2009): in the 19th century, excluding women from politics was treated as a mark of a civilised state. Later the standard reversed, and women's political inclusion became a sign of an advanced state. Norms spread through status hierarchies among states.
- Finnemore and Sikkink, "International Norm Dynamics and Political Change" (IO, 1998), describe a norm life cycle: emergence (norm entrepreneurs), a tipping point, then a cascade driven by legitimacy and esteem, and finally internalisation. Women's suffrage is a central example; New Zealand was the first country to grant national suffrage, in 1893.
- Later milestones: CEDAW (1979); UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000) on Women, Peace and Security; "feminist foreign policy" (Sweden 2014–22).

Exam tips: For questions like "Do the rise of human rights and gender equality show a more just order is possible?", combine Moyn's or Sikkink's history with norm-diffusion theory. Then test it against current hard cases (Ukraine, weak ICC enforcement, backlash politics).

notes.h: Power in the global economy and governing the global commons
notes.body:
These lectures bring international political economy (IPE) and environmental politics into the paper. The common question is whether self-interested states can cooperate without a world government, and who holds power when they do.

Power in the global economy
- Hegemonic stability theory: an open world economy needs a leader to provide public goods. Charles Kindleberger, The World in Depression 1929–1939 (1973), argued that the interwar slump deepened because Britain was unable, and the US unwilling, to lead. See also Robert Gilpin, War and Change in World Politics (1981).
- Embedded liberalism (John Ruggie, 1982): the post-1945 Bretton Woods bargain (IMF and World Bank 1944, GATT 1947) combined international openness with domestic welfare and intervention.
- The order changed when the dollar's convertibility into gold ended (1971), the WTO was created (1995) and China joined the WTO (2001).
- Susan Strange, States and Markets (1988), identified structural power in four structures: security, production, finance and knowledge. Structural power is the ability to shape the frameworks within which others act.
- Helen Milner (International Studies Quarterly, 2021): the inequality and insecurity associated with economic openness have fed political backlash in democracies. The question is whether global capitalism and democracy can be reconciled.
- Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman: the "New Interdependence Approach" (2016) treats interdependence as a political structure that creates asymmetric opportunities across borders. "Weaponized Interdependence" (International Security, 2019) shows that states controlling network hubs (the dollar system, SWIFT, internet infrastructure) can use them for surveillance (the "panopticon" effect) and denial (the "chokepoint" effect).
- Examples: cutting Russian banks off from SWIFT (2022); US export controls on advanced semiconductors to China (from October 2022); Chinese controls on critical minerals; and the sweeping US tariffs announced in April 2025.

Governing the global commons
- Key terms. Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival (e.g. a stable climate). Common-pool resources are non-excludable but rival (e.g. fisheries).
- Collective-action problem: Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965), on free-riding. Garrett Hardin, "The Tragedy of the Commons" (Science, 1968), argued that open access leads to overuse unless there is privatisation or state control.
- Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990), showed that communities often govern commons successfully through self-organised institutions. Her design principles include clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective-choice arrangements, monitoring, graduated sanctions, conflict-resolution mechanisms, recognition of the right to organise, and nested enterprises. She shared the Nobel economics prize in 2009.
- Scott Barrett (Environmental and Resource Economics, 1998): with no world government, environmental treaties must be self-enforcing. Broad participation usually comes at the cost of shallow commitments. The Montreal Protocol (1987) on ozone-depleting substances succeeded because costs were manageable and it used trade restrictions against non-parties. It was the first UN treaty to achieve universal ratification.
- Climate regime: the Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding targets for developed states only. The Paris Agreement (2015) relies on bottom-up nationally determined contributions (NDCs), reviewed and ratcheted every five years, aiming to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C.
- Recent developments: the US left Paris (effective November 2020), rejoined in 2021 and left again, with effect from 27 January 2026. In July 2025 the International Court of Justice gave an advisory opinion that states have legal obligations to address climate change.

Theory link: realists stress relative gains and power, so they are sceptical of climate cooperation. Liberal institutionalists stress regime design (Keohane, Barrett). Constructivists stress changing norms (e.g. "net zero"). Ostrom shows that self-governance below the state level can work.

Exam tips: A past question asked whether commons problems are better solved by self-interested cooperation or by changing norms. Use Montreal and Paris as contrasting cases, and bring in Ostrom to challenge the Hardin dichotomy.

notes.h: The crisis of the liberal international order?
notes.body:
The paper ends with a live debate: is the US-led liberal international order (LIO) in terminal decline, and what might replace it? It looks in turn at challenges from within the West, from Russia and other discontented states, and from China and alternative visions.

What is the LIO?
- The order built after 1945 under US leadership, and extended after 1991, combines open markets, multilateral institutions (UN, IMF, World Bank, GATT/WTO), alliances (NATO, US alliances in Asia), and promotion of democracy and human rights. G. John Ikenberry, Liberal Leviathan (2011).
- Critics note that it was never fully global or fully liberal. It coexisted with empire, Cold War interventions and racial hierarchy.

The West: crisis from within
- Jeff Colgan and Robert Keohane, "The Liberal Order Is Rigged" (Foreign Affairs, 2017): the order delivered for elites and corporations while neglecting those left behind by globalisation. This fed populist backlash, so it must be reformed or it will wither.
- Ikenberry, "The End of Liberal International Order?" (International Affairs, 2018): this is a crisis of governance and authority, not the death of liberal internationalism. The order's underlying logic remains attractive.
- John Mearsheimer, "Bound to Fail" (International Security, 2019): the post-Cold War order of liberal hegemony was always doomed by overreach and nationalism. A realist order of great-power competition is returning.
- Evidence: the Brexit referendum (2016); Donald Trump's elections (2016, 2024) and second term from 20 January 2025, with sweeping tariffs (April 2025) and US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement (effective 27 January 2026) and the WHO (effective 22 January 2026); and NATO's 2025 Hague summit pledge to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP by 2035.

Russia and other discontents
- Grievance and status: Putin's Munich speech (2007) attacked US unipolarity. War with Georgia followed (2008), then Crimea (2014) and the full-scale invasion of Ukraine (24 February 2022). As of October 2026 the war is unresolved.
- Explanations: NATO enlargement as provocation (Mearsheimer, "Why the Ukraine Crisis Is the West's Fault", Foreign Affairs, 2014); imperial revanchism and regime security; and status-seeking (Larson and Shevchenko, "Status Seekers", International Security, 2010).
- Stigma and mimicry: Kurowska and Reshetnikov (EJIR, 2021) describe Russian "trickstery". Russia mimics and parodies Western liberal norms, for example citing Kosovo or self-determination to justify Crimea, exposing double standards rather than simply rejecting the norms.
- Rebecca Adler-Nissen and Ayşe Zarakol, "Struggles for Recognition" (International Organization, 2021): discontents inside and outside the West share grievances about the order's status hierarchies, and these struggles for recognition are merging.
- Many states in the Global South have refused to take sides over Ukraine, reflecting resentment at Western double standards.

China and alternative orders
- China's rise: WTO entry (2001); the Belt and Road Initiative (2013); the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (operating from 2016); the Global Development (2021), Global Security (2022) and Global Civilization (2023) Initiatives; and a Global Governance Initiative announced at the SCO-plus meeting in Tianjin (September 2025).
- Debates:
  - Power transition and the "Thucydides Trap" (Graham Allison, Destined for War, 2017) see danger as a rising power nears an established one.
  - Ikenberry (2008) argued the Western order is "hard to overturn and easy to join", so China might rise within it.
  - Michael Beckley and Hal Brands (Danger Zone, 2022) argue that a peaking China facing slowdown may be more dangerous than a rising one.
- Amitav Acharya, "After Liberal Hegemony" (Ethics & International Affairs, 2017): a "multiplex" world is emerging. Like a multiplex cinema, it has many shows and no single director. Power is spread among states, regional institutions and non-state actors, rather than forming a simple multipolarity.
- Other Asian visions: India's "multi-alignment", and a 2023 International Affairs special issue on Asian conceptions of international order.
- BRICS expanded in 2024 (Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE) and 2025 (Indonesia).

Exam tips: Avoid treating "the West versus the rest" as a single cleavage. Past questions have asked whether challenges to the LIO prove constructivism wrong and realism right. A good answer shows that status, recognition and identity (constructivist themes) are central to Russian and Chinese grievances, even where the stakes are about power.

cards.f: Bull and Watson, The Expansion of International Society (1984)
cards.b: Classic English School account: a European society of sovereign states formed first and then expanded to cover the globe. POL2 treats it as the Eurocentric story to be challenged.

The 19th-century criteria (legal system, ability to protect foreigners, diplomatic practice) that non-European states had to meet to be admitted to European international society. Analysed by Gerrit Gong (1984).

A hierarchical system of relations centred on the Chinese emperor. Foreign rulers sent missions and performed ritual deference in return for trade and recognition. Europeans arriving from 1513 had to work within it.
British mission to the Qianlong emperor seeking wider trade and a permanent embassy. It was turned down, which shows that Europeans were not dominant in East Asia before the 19th century.

cards.f: Clulow, The Company and the Shogun (2014)
cards.b: Shows that the Dutch East India Company, which behaved like a sovereign in much of Asia, had to accept a subordinate, vassal-like role under the Tokugawa shogunate in Japan.
Artificial island at Nagasaki where the Dutch were confined from 1641. A symbol of Tokugawa control over European contact.

In Spanish–Nahua interaction after the conquest, each side assumed a given form or concept worked as it did in its own tradition. These convergent misreadings let Nahua structures persist under Spanish guise.

Treaties of Münster and Osnabrück that ended the Thirty Years' War (1618–48); Spain also recognised the Dutch Republic. Often, controversially, treated as the founding moment of the sovereign states system.

Argues the 1648 treaties dealt mainly with the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire, did not create sovereignty, and made France and Sweden guarantors, which is closer to intervention than to non-intervention.

cards.f: Spruyt, The Sovereign State and Its Competitors (1994)
cards.b: Territorial states beat city-leagues and city-states because they were better at internal rationalisation (coinage, law), curbing free-riders and making credible external commitments, and because rulers preferred to recognise similar units.
'War made the state, and the state made war' (1975). Rulers who could extract men and money to fight survived. Coercion, Capital, and European States, AD 990–1990 (1990) traces different paths.
Stephen Krasner's claim that rulers routinely violate Westphalian sovereignty (non-interference in domestic authority) when it suits them, while still professing the norm.

'Whose realm, his religion': the principle of the Peace of Augsburg (1555) letting rulers in the Empire choose their territory's confession. Westphalia modified it with 1624 as a protective 'normative year'.
Jean Bodin, Six Livres de la République (1576), and Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), theorised supreme, undivided authority within a polity: the conceptual basis of internal sovereignty.
Argues Spanish American independence was the dissolution of a transatlantic Spanish Monarchy, triggered by Napoleon's invasion of Spain (1808), not simply an anticolonial nationalist revolt.

Latin America's mostly 'limited wars' meant states did not build strong extractive capacity; governments relied on customs revenues and foreign loans. A challenge to applying Tilly's thesis outside Europe.
Revolution of 1791–1804 in French Saint-Domingue. Haiti became independent in 1804 as the first state founded by formerly enslaved people.

California School text: the Yangzi Delta and England were comparable until c.1800. Britain diverged thanks to accessible coal and New World resources ('ghost acres') rather than deep cultural superiority.
Meeting of European powers (plus the US and the Ottoman Empire) that set rules for claiming African territory, part of the 'Scramble for Africa'.

cards.f: Barnhart (2016) on the Scramble for Africa
cards.b: Humiliated states seek territory to restore status. If they cannot retaliate against the stronger humiliator, they seize land elsewhere, e.g. France taking Tunisia (1881) after defeat in 1870–71.
Gallagher and Robinson (1953): Britain preferred informal influence through trade, finance and treaties, using formal annexation only when informal means failed.
Founding text of neorealism. Structure = ordering principle (anarchy), function of units (like units) and distribution of capabilities. Predicts self-help and balancing; saw bipolarity as stable.
Measures one state takes to increase its own security (arms, alliances) reduce others' security, producing spirals of mistrust even among defensive states. Herz (1950); Jervis (1978).
Liberal states maintain a 'separate peace' among themselves, while remaining capable of war and imprudence towards non-liberal states. Builds on Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795).

Neoliberal institutionalism: even rational egoist states under anarchy cooperate through regimes, which reduce transaction costs, supply information and lengthen the shadow of the future, outlasting a hegemon's decline.

cards.f: Wendt, 'Anarchy is What States Make of It' (1992)
cards.b: Constructivist argument that self-help is not a necessary result of anarchy. It is produced by interaction and shared ideas. Later: Hobbesian, Lockean and Kantian cultures of anarchy (1999).
Security of identity: states need stable routines and self-understanding, so they may cling to familiar conflictual relationships, which helps explain persistent security dilemmas.
Ruggie's label for the shared rationalist core of neorealism and neoliberal institutionalism, which take state identities and interests as given. Constructivism asks how they are constituted.
Classical realist critique of interwar 'utopianism': appeals to a universal harmony of interests disguised the interests of satisfied ('have') powers.
1930s framing of revisionist powers (Germany, Italy, Japan) as lacking land, colonies and raw materials against satisfied status-quo powers (Britain, France, US). Discussed by Carr (1939).

Economic history of Nazi Germany. Argues Hitler measured Germany against the United States and sought continental scale before American power became overwhelming; rearmament pressures shaped the timing of war.

Japan's proposal at the Paris Peace Conference to add racial equality to the League Covenant. It was not adopted. Shimazu (1998) stresses Japan's concern with its own great-power status and equal treatment for its nationals abroad.
Set a 5:5:3 ratio of capital ships for the US, Britain and Japan, which many in Japan saw as a sign of unequal status.
Non-aggression pact of 23 August 1939 between Germany and the USSR, with secret protocols dividing Eastern Europe. Broken by Operation Barbarossa on 22 June 1941.
US former Secretary of State Dean Acheson said Britain had 'lost an empire and has not yet found a role', a touchstone for debates about Britain's post-imperial global role.
W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk: 'the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line'. Used to frame the century's conflicts as struggles over racial hierarchy.
George Kennan's cable from Moscow analysing Soviet behaviour. With his 1947 'X' article it underpinned the US strategy of containment.

cards.f: Jervis, 'Was the Cold War a Security Dilemma?' (2001)
cards.b: Answer: largely not. Despite spiral elements, its root was a clash of social systems and visions of order, so mutual security was hard to achieve until Soviet policy changed fundamentally.
Early nuclear strategy text: from now on the chief purpose of military establishments must be to avert wars, not win them. The foundation of deterrence thinking.
Condition in which each side has a secure second-strike capability, so any nuclear first strike would bring unacceptable retaliation. Credited with stabilising superpower relations.
The absence of great-power war after 1945, explained by bipolarity, nuclear deterrence and shared 'rules of the game'.
Material explanation of the Cold War's end: Soviet relative decline and the globalisation of production raised the costs of isolation, pushing Soviet leaders towards retrenchment.
Gorbachev takes power March 1985; INF Treaty 1987; Berlin Wall falls 9 Nov 1989; German reunification 3 Oct 1990; USSR dissolved 26 Dec 1991.
The last US–Russian treaty capping deployed strategic nuclear forces expired on 5 February 2026 without a replacement agreement.
After major wars (1815, 1919, 1945) leading states can bind themselves in institutions ('strategic restraint') to reassure others. This produced the highly institutionalised post-1945 order.
Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples: affirmed self-determination and called for a speedy end to colonialism.

Anticolonial nationalists (Nkrumah, Nyerere, Eric Williams, Manley) sought to remake international order: self-determination as a human right, regional federations and the New International Economic Order.
Negative: legal freedom from outside interference. Positive: the capacity to govern and deliver public goods. Jackson called states with only the former 'quasi-states'.
Intervention norms change over time: forcible debt collection became illegitimate, humanitarian concern widened to non-Europeans, and multilateral authorisation became expected.

ICISS report (2001); endorsed at the 2005 UN World Summit. States must protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity; the international community may act through the Security Council if they fail.
51 founding members in 1945; 193 today (South Sudan joined in 2011). Most of the growth reflects decolonisation, e.g. 17 African states becoming independent in 1960.
Argues human rights only became a powerful global movement in the 1970s, after other utopias (socialism, anticolonial nationalism) faded, not in the 1940s.
Rebuts human rights pessimism: rights have longer, more global (including Latin American) origins and, measured carefully, have improved outcomes over time.
Prohibits 'the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state'. Exceptions: self-defence (Art. 51) and Security Council action under Chapter VII.

cards.f: Fazal, 'Why States No Longer Declare War' (2012)
cards.b: Formal war declarations have nearly vanished since 1945 because codified humanitarian law makes acknowledging war costly. States avoid triggering those obligations.
Since 1945, especially after the mid-1970s, successful conquest and forcible border change have become rare and annexations go unrecognised.
Norm emergence (entrepreneurs), tipping point, norm cascade (socialisation, legitimacy, esteem), internalisation. Women's suffrage is a key illustration.

cards.f: Towns (2009) on the status of women
cards.b: In the 19th century, excluding women from politics marked a 'civilised' state; later women's inclusion became the marker of an advanced state. Norms spread via status hierarchies.
General Assembly resolution condemning Russia's attempted annexation of four Ukrainian regions; adopted by 143 votes to 5, with 35 abstentions.

An open world economy needs a dominant power to supply public goods (open markets, a lender of last resort). Kindleberger (1973): the 1930s slump deepened because Britain was unable and the US unwilling to lead.
The post-1945 bargain combining multilateral economic openness with domestic welfare and state intervention, institutionalised at Bretton Woods.
States controlling hubs in global networks (dollar clearing, SWIFT, internet) can exploit them: 'panopticon' effects (information) and 'chokepoint' effects (denying access).
Power to shape the frameworks in which others operate, exercised through four structures: security, production, finance and knowledge.
Communities often manage common-pool resources sustainably through self-organised rules (boundaries, monitoring, graduated sanctions, etc.), challenging the state-or-market dichotomy.
Open-access resources tend to be overused because each user gains the full benefit of extra use but bears only part of the cost; Hardin proposed privatisation or state control.
Treaty phasing out ozone-depleting substances. Seen as the model of successful environmental cooperation (trade restrictions on non-parties, funding for developing states); universally ratified.
Climate treaty built on bottom-up nationally determined contributions, reviewed every five years; aims for well below 2°C and to pursue 1.5°C. US withdrawal took effect on 27 January 2026.
US-led order after 1945 (extended after 1991): open markets, multilateral institutions, alliances, democracy and human rights. Ikenberry, Liberal Leviathan (2011).

cards.f: Colgan and Keohane, 'The Liberal Order Is Rigged' (2017)
cards.b: Argue the order served elites and corporations while neglecting globalisation's losers, fuelling populism; liberals must reform it or watch it wither.
Realist argument that the post-Cold War liberal order was doomed by overreach (spreading democracy, enlarging institutions) and nationalism; great-power competition returns.

Post-hegemonic order likened to a multiplex cinema: many shows, no single director. Power and ideas are dispersed among states, regions and non-state actors, rather than forming a classic multipolarity.
Graham Allison's claim that when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, war is a serious risk; based on historical cases of power transition.
Danger Zone: a China whose rise is slowing may act aggressively while it still can, so its decline, not just its rise, threatens peace.
Russia mimics and parodies Western liberal norms (e.g. invoking Kosovo or self-determination over Crimea) to expose double standards and evade stigma.
Belt and Road (2013); Global Development (2021), Global Security (2022) and Global Civilization (2023) Initiatives; Global Governance Initiative (Tianjin, September 2025).

questions.q: Which statement best captures the aim of starting POL2 in c.1500?
options: To show that the modern state system was fully formed by 1500
To decentre Europe by showing several international orders coexisting, with Europeans often weak newcomers
To argue that non-European polities had no international relations before European contact
To focus on the diplomatic history of the Holy Roman Empire
questions.why: The paper's global, historical approach is meant to show plural early modern orders (Chinese, Japanese, Ottoman, Mughal) in which Europeans were often supplicants. The modern state system was not formed by 1500. Saying non-Europeans had no international relations is the very Eurocentric assumption the paper criticises. The Holy Roman Empire belongs to the Westphalia lecture and is far too narrow a focus.

questions.q: What does Adam Clulow's study of the Dutch in Tokugawa Japan mainly show?
options: The VOC forced Japan open to free trade by naval power
The VOC had to recast itself as a subordinate of the shogun, despite acting as a sovereign elsewhere in Asia
Japan adopted European ideas of sovereignty in the 17th century
The Dutch were expelled from Japan in 1641 and never returned
questions.why: Clulow's argument is that the Company, a sovereign-like actor elsewhere, had to adapt to Japanese hierarchy and act as a loyal vassal. Japan was forced open by the United States in the 1850s, not by the VOC. Japan did not adopt European sovereignty ideas in the 1600s. The Dutch were not expelled in 1641: they were moved to Dejima and stayed.

questions.q: Was European expansion before c.1800 'colonial'? Give a brief argued answer using two regions.
markScheme: Defines 'colonial' (territorial rule, settlement and/or political subordination of local societies)
Americas: conquest of the Mexica and Inca, settlement and coerced labour show a colonial pattern
East Asia: Europeans worked within Chinese and Japanese rules (Macartney 1793; the VOC at Dejima), so the relationship was not colonial
Concludes that the answer varies by region and period, and avoids reading later 19th-century dominance backwards
Uses at least one named scholar (e.g. Clulow, Zhang, Lockhart) accurately
questions.modelAnswer: It depends on where we look. If 'colonial' means territorial rule and the subordination of local societies, the Americas fit: the Spanish conquest of the Mexica (1519–21) and the Inca (from 1532) led to settlement, coerced labour and demographic collapse. Even there, Lockhart shows that indigenous structures and perspectives continued. In East Asia the picture is reversed. Zhang describes Europeans as supplicants in the Chinese order, and the Macartney mission (1793) was turned away. Clulow shows the VOC acting as a subordinate of the Tokugawa shogun, confined to Dejima from 1641. Before c.1800, then, 'colonial' fits the Atlantic world much better than Asia, and calling the whole period colonial reads later European dominance backwards.

questions.q: Which claim is central to the 'Westphalian myth' critique?
options: The 1648 treaties abolished the Holy Roman Empire
The 1648 treaties mainly regulated the Holy Roman Empire's constitution and did not establish sovereignty or non-intervention
The 1648 treaties were signed only by Protestant powers
Westphalia created the United Nations' principle of sovereign equality directly
questions.why: Osiander and Beaulac argue that the treaties concerned imperial constitutional arrangements, and that the sovereignty story was read back later. The Empire was not abolished: it lasted until 1806. Catholic powers such as France and the Emperor were central parties, so it was not a Protestant-only settlement. Sovereign equality as a UN principle comes from the 1945 Charter, not directly from 1648.

questions.q: According to Hendrik Spruyt, why did the sovereign territorial state displace its competitors?
options: Solely because it won more wars than city-states
Because the Church granted it legal supremacy in 1648
Because it was institutionally more effective and other actors preferred to recognise similar units
Because city-leagues voluntarily dissolved after the Black Death
questions.why: Spruyt stresses selection through institutional efficiency (standard coinage and law, fewer free-riders, credible commitments) plus mutual recognition among like units. War alone is closer to Tilly, and Spruyt explicitly rejects a purely war-based account. No papal grant of supremacy happened in 1648. City-leagues did not simply dissolve themselves after the plague.

questions.q: Explain two reasons why IR scholars call the Westphalian story a 'myth', and one reason it still matters.
markScheme: Treaties concerned the Holy Roman Empire's internal constitution and the estates' rights, not a new sovereign states system (Osiander 2001)
Guarantor roles for France and Sweden, and religious protections (1624 normative year), contradict the idea of non-intervention
The 'Westphalian' label was built later by international lawyers and theorists such as Vattel (1758) and 19th-century writers (Beaulac 2000)
Still matters as a constitutive idea: it shapes how IR theory defines the system and how states (e.g. China, Russia) justify non-interference
Clear, accurate use of dates and authors
questions.modelAnswer: First, the treaties of Münster and Osnabrück (1648) were mainly about the constitution of the Holy Roman Empire, which survived until 1806. They did not announce a world of sovereign states (Osiander 2001). Second, the settlement built in external involvement. France and Sweden became guarantors of the imperial settlement, and the religious clauses protected rights as they stood in the 'normative year' of 1624, limiting rulers rather than freeing them. Beaulac adds that the 'Westphalian' orthodoxy was constructed later by lawyers such as Vattel. Even so, the myth matters. Ideas shape practice: states still appeal to 'Westphalian' non-interference, as China and Russia do, and IR theory's picture of anarchy among like units rests on it.

questions.q: Which argument is associated with Miguel Centeno's Blood and Debt?
options: Frequent total wars made Latin American states unusually strong
Latin America's limited wars meant states relied on customs revenue and loans rather than building strong extractive capacity
Latin American states were created mainly by the Berlin Conference
Spanish American independence was caused by the Great Divergence
questions.why: Centeno argues that the absence of Tilly-style total war left Latin American states fiscally and institutionally weaker, dependent on loans and customs duties. The claim about frequent total wars is the reverse of his argument. The Berlin Conference concerned Africa. Centeno's book is about war and state-building after independence, not the causes of independence, and the Great Divergence is Pomeranz's topic.

questions.q: What do the 'ghost acres' in Pomeranz's account of the Great Divergence refer to?
options: Land lost to European states through war
The extra land-equivalent resources Britain gained from New World colonies
Uncultivated land in the Yangzi Delta
Territory claimed but never occupied in the Scramble for Africa
questions.why: Pomeranz uses 'ghost acres' for the land-equivalent resources (e.g. cotton, sugar, timber) Britain drew from the Americas, easing its ecological constraints. Land lost in war plays no part in his argument. The idea is not about uncultivated Chinese land. Paper claims in Africa belong to the later Scramble, not to Pomeranz's explanation.

questions.q: Briefly assess whether violence was necessary to the making of nations in the Americas.
markScheme: Notes the centrality of independence wars and wars against indigenous peoples (e.g. US removal, the Conquest of the Desert)
Uses Rodríguez to show that political collapse (1808) and constitutional politics (Cádiz 1812) mattered as well as fighting
Uses Centeno to show that Latin America's limited interstate wars produced weaker states, so war was not the main state-builder
Distinguishes nation-building (identity) from state-building (institutions)
Reaches a qualified judgement
questions.modelAnswer: Violence was pervasive but not the whole story. Independence was won through war, and both the United States and Argentina expanded through violent campaigns against indigenous peoples, such as removal after 1830 and the 'Conquest of the Desert'. Yet Rodríguez shows that Spanish American independence began with the collapse of the Spanish Monarchy after Napoleon's 1808 invasion and with constitutional politics at Cádiz (1812), not with pre-formed nations fighting their way out. Centeno adds that Latin America's mostly limited interstate wars did not build strong states. Governments borrowed instead of taxing, so war was a weak state-maker there. Violence was therefore necessary to territorial nation-making, but political and fiscal processes shaped what kind of states emerged.

questions.q: Which feature is NOT one of the three elements of Waltz's definition of international structure?
options: Ordering principle (anarchy)
Character of units' domestic regimes
Function of units (like units)
Distribution of capabilities
questions.why: Waltz deliberately leaves domestic regime type out of structure: that is second-image (unit-level) reasoning. Anarchy as ordering principle, like units with similar functions, and the distribution of capabilities are the three elements he does include.

questions.q: Jennifer Mitzen's concept of ontological security helps explain…
options: why democracies never fight each other
why states may persist in costly conflicts that provide a stable sense of identity
why hegemons create international regimes
why bipolar systems are more stable than multipolar ones
questions.why: Mitzen argues that states seek stable identities and routines, so they can become attached to conflictual relationships. The claim that democracies do not fight each other is the liberal or democratic peace (Doyle), not ontological security. Regime creation by hegemons belongs to hegemonic stability and Keohane. The claim about bipolar stability is Waltz's.

questions.q: Compare realism and constructivism on whether anarchy makes conflict inevitable.
markScheme: Neorealism (Waltz): anarchy plus self-help produce balancing and recurrent conflict; the security dilemma (Herz, Jervis)
Classical realism grounds conflict partly in human nature (Morgenthau), and Williams adds a stress on prudence and limits
Constructivism (Wendt 1992): anarchy has no fixed logic; Hobbesian, Lockean and Kantian cultures are possible
Ruggie or Mitzen: identities and norms shape interests, and conflict may persist for identity reasons, not structure alone
Example or evaluation (e.g. the Kantian culture among Western states after 1945; the persistence of the Cold War)
questions.modelAnswer: For Waltz, anarchy, the absence of a higher authority, forces states to rely on self-help. Because one state's security measures threaten others (the security dilemma of Herz and Jervis), competition and balancing recur, though war is not certain at every moment. Wendt replies that 'anarchy is what states make of it'. Self-help is a product of interaction and shared ideas, so anarchy can sustain Hobbesian enmity, Lockean rivalry or Kantian friendship. Relations among Western democracies after 1945 look Kantian. Mitzen adds that conflict can persist because states need stable identities, not just because of structure. On this view conflict is possible but not inevitable. Realists counter that ideas can change faster than capabilities, so prudence still calls for hedging.

questions.q: What did Japan's 1919 Racial Equality Proposal mainly seek, on Naoko Shimazu's reading?
options: A universal end to colonial rule
Recognition of Japan's equal great-power status and equal treatment for Japanese nationals abroad
Japanese withdrawal from the League of Nations
Equal naval tonnage with Britain
questions.why: Shimazu stresses status and the treatment of Japanese nationals abroad rather than a universal programme. A universal end to colonial rule is wrong because Japan was itself an imperial power (Taiwan, Korea). Withdrawal from the League came in 1933 over Manchuria. Naval ratios were the business of the 1922 Washington Treaty.

questions.q: Which date pairing is correct?
options: Operation Barbarossa – 22 June 1941
Pearl Harbor – 7 December 1940
Nazi–Soviet Pact – 23 August 1938
Japan leaves the League of Nations – 1937
questions.why: Germany invaded the USSR on 22 June 1941. Pearl Harbor was attacked on 7 December 1941, not 1940. The Nazi–Soviet Pact was signed on 23 August 1939. Japan left the League in 1933, after the Manchurian crisis; 1937 is when its full-scale war with China began.

questions.q: How far does the interwar Japanese challenge to Anglo-American order resemble China's challenge today? Identify two similarities and one difference.
markScheme: Similarity: a rising Asian power seeking status and recognition in an order shaped by Anglo-American power (1919 proposal and 5:5:3 ratio as status grievances)
Similarity: a regional order project (Co-Prosperity Sphere then; Belt and Road Initiative and regional institutions now) and naval build-up

Difference: Japan pursued conquest and formal empire in the 1930s, whereas China has largely pursued influence through economic means and institutions; or nuclear weapons and economic interdependence change the stakes
Accurate dates and examples
questions.modelAnswer: There are real parallels. Both are rising Asian powers that resent an order built around Anglo-American power and seek recognition. Japan's rebuff over racial equality in 1919 and the 5:5:3 naval ratio (1922) were felt as status humiliations, much as Chinese leaders speak of past humiliation and demand a greater say. Both also pursue regional order projects backed by naval power: then the Co-Prosperity Sphere (1940), now the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), new institutions and a fast-growing navy. The key difference is method and context. 1930s Japan used conquest (Manchuria 1931, China 1937). China today operates within deep economic interdependence and under nuclear deterrence, and has mostly pursued influence through economic and institutional means, though tensions over Taiwan and the South China Sea remain.

questions.q: What is Robert Jervis's verdict in 'Was the Cold War a Security Dilemma?' (2001)?
options: Yes: it was a pure spiral produced by mutual misperception between defensive states
Largely no: its root was a clash of incompatible social systems and visions of order
Yes: nuclear weapons alone created the security dilemma
No: the Cold War was caused purely by US economic expansionism
questions.why: Jervis acknowledges spiral elements but argues that the conflict was rooted in genuinely incompatible goals, so mutual security was elusive until Soviet policy changed. A pure misperception spiral is exactly what he rejects. He does not make nuclear weapons the sole cause. The claim that US expansion alone caused the Cold War is the revisionist thesis of W.A. Williams, not Jervis.

questions.q: Which treaty opened for signature in 1968 and aims to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons?
options: The INF Treaty
The Partial Test Ban Treaty
The Non-Proliferation Treaty
New START
questions.why: The NPT was signed in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. The INF Treaty (1987) eliminated intermediate-range missiles. The Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963) banned atmospheric, underwater and outer-space tests. New START (2010) limited US and Russian strategic forces and expired in 2026.

questions.q: Compare a material and an ideational explanation of the end of the Cold War.
markScheme: Material: relative Soviet economic decline and globalisation of production made isolation costly (Brooks and Wohlforth 2000/01)
Ideational: Gorbachev's 'new thinking' and changing Soviet identity, plus transnational networks (Evangelista; English)
Shows how the explanations differ on timing and on choice (why reform, not repression)
Evaluation: the two may be complementary, and process tracing can help adjudicate (Evangelista 2014)
Accurate dates (1985, 1989, 1991)
questions.modelAnswer: Brooks and Wohlforth argue that the Soviet Union's relative economic decline, together with the globalisation of production, made continued isolation and confrontation increasingly costly. Retrenchment was therefore a rational response to material pressure. Ideational accounts reply that decline does not dictate a response. Previous Soviet leaders had repressed rather than reformed, and it took Gorbachev's 'new thinking' after March 1985, shaped by transnational contacts with Western scientists and activists (Evangelista) and a changing Soviet identity (English), to choose withdrawal from Eastern Europe and accept the fall of the Wall in 1989. The best answer combines them: material decline created the problem, while ideas shaped the peaceful solution. Evangelista shows how process tracing can test which mattered at each step.

questions.q: Robert Jackson's 'quasi-states' are states that…
options: lack legal recognition but have strong administrative capacity
have negative sovereignty guaranteed by international norms but limited positive sovereignty
are formally part of a federation such as the West Indies Federation
have been suspended from the United Nations
questions.why: Jackson's quasi-states enjoy juridical (negative) sovereignty protected by international norms but lack empirical (positive) capacity. Having capacity without recognition is the reverse of his concept. Federations are a separate topic, linked to Getachew. UN suspension has nothing to do with the idea.

questions.q: Which intervention went ahead without explicit UN Security Council authorisation?
options: NATO's Kosovo campaign (1999)
The Libya intervention under Resolution 1973 (2011)
The Korean War response (1950)
The 1991 Gulf War to reverse Iraq's invasion of Kuwait
questions.why: NATO's 1999 Kosovo bombing lacked Security Council authorisation, which is why it is often described as 'illegal but legitimate'. Libya in 2011 was authorised by Resolution 1973. Korea in 1950 was backed by Council resolutions passed while the USSR was absent. The 1991 Gulf War was authorised by Resolution 678.

questions.q: What caused decolonisation after 1945? Give three causes and evaluate their relative weight.
markScheme: Metropolitan factors: economic cost, war exhaustion and a changing imperial calculus
Peripheral agency: nationalist mobilisation and wars (e.g. Algeria 1954–62, Indochina 1954); Getachew's worldmaking
International and normative factors: superpower anticolonialism, the UN and self-determination as a norm (UNGA 1514, 1960); Reus-Smit on rights struggles
Evaluation, e.g. normative change made empire illegitimate, while nationalist pressure determined timing
Accurate examples and dates
questions.modelAnswer: Three sets of causes interacted. First, in the metropoles, Britain and France were exhausted and indebted after 1945, and the cost of holding empire rose. Second, colonised peoples organised. Mass nationalist movements and wars of independence, from Indochina (Dien Bien Phu, 1954) to Algeria (1954–62), made rule unsustainable. Getachew shows that leaders such as Nkrumah also pursued a wider project of remaking international order. Third, the international setting changed. Both superpowers opposed old-style colonialism, and self-determination hardened into a norm at the UN with Resolution 1514 (1960). Reus-Smit links expansion of the system to struggles for individual rights. Material weakness explains why empires could be given up, but anticolonial agency and the new legitimacy of self-determination explain the speed and scale, as seen in 1960.

questions.q: What is Tanisha Fazal's explanation for the decline of formal declarations of war?
options: Nuclear weapons made war impossible
The growth of codified humanitarian law makes formally declaring war costly
The UN Security Council now declares wars on states' behalf
Democracies are constitutionally barred from declaring war
questions.why: Fazal argues that states avoid declarations to escape the legal obligations triggered by codified jus in bello. Wars still occur, so nuclear weapons have not made them impossible. The Security Council authorises force but does not declare war for states. No general constitutional bar on declaring war exists in democracies.

questions.q: Which claim is central to Samuel Moyn's The Last Utopia?
options: Human rights have been a continuous Western tradition since the French Revolution
The UDHR of 1948 immediately launched a mass global movement
Human rights broke through as a powerful movement in the 1970s, after rival utopias faded
Human rights have been proven ineffective by quantitative evidence
questions.why: Moyn's thesis is a 1970s breakthrough. He rejects the idea of a continuous tradition and argues that the 1940s declarations had little practical life, so the claim about 1948 is wrong. The claim about quantitative evidence of failure is not his: debates over effectiveness are Sikkink's terrain, and she argues the opposite.

questions.q: Did Russia's invasion of Ukraine mark the end of the territorial integrity norm?
markScheme: States the norm (Zacher 2001; UN Charter Art. 2(4)): conquest rare and unrecognised since 1945
Evidence of erosion: annexation of Crimea (2014) and four regions (2022); great-power violation by a permanent Security Council member
Evidence of persistence: widespread non-recognition and condemnation (UNGA ES-11/4, 143 votes in favour); sanctions; support for Ukraine
Notes that a norm can survive violations if violators are condemned and still seek to justify their actions (Russia's legal pretexts)
Current status stated accurately (war ongoing as of October 2026, no settlement)
questions.modelAnswer: Zacher's territorial integrity norm holds that since 1945 forcible border change has become rare and annexations go unrecognised. Russia's annexation of Crimea (2014) and its claimed annexation of four Ukrainian regions in September 2022 are serious violations, all the more so because they come from a permanent member of the Security Council. Yet violation alone does not end a norm. The UN General Assembly condemned the 2022 annexations by 143 votes to 5 (ES-11/4), almost no state recognises them, and Russia itself offered legal-sounding justifications such as referendums and self-defence, which shows the norm still constrains how force is presented. As of October 2026 the war continues without a settlement. The norm is damaged, and a negotiated outcome rewarding conquest would weaken it further, but it has not been abandoned.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects Elinor Ostrom's contribution?
options: Common-pool resources can only be saved by privatisation
Communities can often govern common-pool resources sustainably through self-organised institutions
