Only a hegemon can solve collective-action problems
Common-pool resources are non-rival goods
questions.why: Ostrom documented successful self-governance and derived design principles from it. Privatisation is one of the two remedies (with state control) proposed by Hardin, which Ostrom challenged. The claim that only a hegemon can solve such problems is hegemonic stability theory. Common-pool resources are rival (one person's use reduces another's), even though exclusion is hard.

questions.q: In Farrell and Newman's 'weaponized interdependence', the 'chokepoint' effect refers to…
options: a hub state gathering information on flows through a network
a hub state denying others access to a network it controls
a rising power building a rival alliance
a commons being overused by free-riders
questions.why: The chokepoint effect means using control of a hub to deny access, as with cutting banks off from SWIFT. Gathering information through a hub is the separate 'panopticon' effect. Building a rival alliance is balancing, and overuse of a commons is Hardin's tragedy; neither is part of this concept.

questions.q: Why was the Montreal Protocol more successful than international efforts on climate change?
markScheme: Collective-action framing: free-riding and the need for self-enforcing agreements (Barrett 1998)
Montreal: concentrated sources, available substitutes, manageable costs, trade restrictions on non-parties and funding for developing states
Climate: diffuse emissions across all sectors, high and unevenly distributed costs, long time horizons; Kyoto's binding but narrow approach
Paris's bottom-up NDC model gains participation at the cost of depth; US withdrawal (effective January 2026) shows fragility
Theoretical evaluation (liberal institutionalist design vs realist relative gains vs norm change)
questions.modelAnswer: Both are collective-action problems in which states benefit whether or not they contribute. Barrett stresses that, absent world government, agreements must be self-enforcing. Montreal (1987) met that test. Ozone-depleting substances came from a small number of industries, substitutes existed, costs were modest, and the treaty restricted trade with non-parties and funded developing countries, making participation attractive and defection costly. Climate change is much harder. Emissions arise from almost every economic activity, abatement costs are large and unequally spread, and benefits come decades later. Kyoto (1997) bound only developed states. Paris (2015) secured near-universal participation through voluntary NDCs, but commitments are shallow and reversible, as shown by the US withdrawal effective 27 January 2026. Institutional design matters, but structural features of the problem matter more.

questions.q: Which author argued that the liberal international order is in a crisis of governance and authority but not at its end?
options: John Mearsheimer
G. John Ikenberry
Graham Allison
Kenneth Waltz
questions.why: Ikenberry (2018) argues that liberal internationalism will outlast the current crisis. Mearsheimer argues the order was 'bound to fail'. Allison writes on the risk of war in power transitions. Waltz's work predates the debate and concerns structural theory.

questions.q: Amitav Acharya's 'multiplex world' differs from classic multipolarity mainly because…
options: it involves only two superpowers
it disperses power across states, regional bodies and non-state actors with no single director
it describes China replacing the US as hegemon
it predicts the return of 19th-century European great-power concert diplomacy
questions.why: A multiplex order stresses dispersed, layered power and agency beyond states. An order with two superpowers is bipolarity. China replacing the US is hegemonic succession, which Acharya rejects as the likely path. The return of a European concert is the 19th-century model he contrasts it with.

questions.q: Is the crisis of the liberal international order mainly driven from inside the West or from outside it?
markScheme: Inside: inequality and backlash (Colgan and Keohane 2017; Milner); Brexit; US tariffs and withdrawals (Paris and WHO, effective January 2026)
Outside: Russia's war in Ukraine; China's rise and alternative initiatives (BRI, GDI/GSI/GCI); BRICS expansion
Uses theory: Mearsheimer (structural failure) vs Ikenberry (resilient crisis of authority) vs Acharya (multiplex)
Judgement, e.g. external challenges matter more because the order's leading state is withdrawing support
Current facts stated accurately
questions.modelAnswer: There is a good case that the decisive pressures are internal. Colgan and Keohane argue the order was 'rigged' towards elites, generating the backlash seen in Brexit (2016) and Trump's elections. Under Trump's second term the US has imposed sweeping tariffs (2025) and left the Paris Agreement and the WHO (effective January 2026). When the order's architect withdraws support, the order weakens from its core. External challenges are real too. Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022) assaults the territorial integrity norm, and China offers alternatives through the Belt and Road Initiative and its global initiatives. Yet these challengers often exploit Western double standards and US retrenchment rather than cause them. Ikenberry's view of a crisis of authority, not collapse, fits best: external rivals are dangerous chiefly because the West's internal consensus has frayed.

questions.q: 'The modern international order was made in Europe and exported to the rest of the world.' Discuss with reference to at least two periods since c.1500.
markScheme: Clear thesis that engages the quotation's two claims (made in Europe; exported) rather than describing history
Early modern: plural orders (Chinese tributary system, Tokugawa Japan, Ottoman and Mughal empires); Europeans as supplicants (Zhang, Clulow, Macartney 1793)
Westphalia as myth (Osiander, Beaulac): even the 'European' origin story is questionable; Spruyt and Tilly on state formation
19th century: the Great Divergence (Pomeranz) and imperialism (Berlin 1884–85; standard of civilisation) give the quotation its strongest support
20th century: decolonisation as co-production, with anticolonial worldmaking (Getachew), self-determination (UNGA 1514) and rights struggles (Reus-Smit) reshaping the order
Contemporary relevance: Acharya's multiplex world; non-Western visions of order; Westphalian rhetoric used by China and Russia
Use of theory (English School expansion thesis vs critics; constructivist accounts of norm diffusion)
Balanced conclusion, accurate dates and authors
questions.modelAnswer:
Thesis: The quotation reflects the English School 'expansion' story of Bull and Watson (1984). It captures the 19th century well but misdescribes both the early modern period and the 20th-century making of today's order. The modern order was co-produced through encounter, conquest and anticolonial resistance.

1. Early modern plural orders. Around 1500 Europe was one region among several. The Chinese tributary order set the terms for Portuguese and later traders. Zhang calls Europeans 'supplicants', and the Macartney mission (1793) was rebuffed. Clulow shows the VOC acting as a subordinate of the Tokugawa shogun, confined to Dejima from 1641. The Ottoman and Mughal empires dealt with Europeans on their own terms. Only in the Americas did encounter become conquest, and even there Lockhart shows indigenous structures persisting.

2. Was the order even 'made in Europe'? The idea that Westphalia (1648) created sovereign states is a myth. Osiander shows the treaties regulated the Holy Roman Empire and built in external guarantees. State formation was a longer process of selection (Spruyt) and war-making (Tilly). Some key features, such as self-determination and universal sovereign equality, were not European achievements at all.

3. The strongest case for the quotation: the 19th century. The Great Divergence (Pomeranz) gave Europe material dominance. The Opium Wars, the Berlin Conference (1884–85) and the 'standard of civilisation' (Gong) imposed European rules globally. Here the order was exported by force.

4. The 20th century: remade by the colonised. Decolonisation took the UN from 51 members to 193. Getachew shows anticolonial leaders such as Nkrumah and Nyerere pursuing 'worldmaking': making self-determination a right (UNGA 1514, 1960), proposing federations and demanding a New International Economic Order (1974). Reus-Smit links the system's expansion to rights struggles in imperial peripheries. Universal sovereignty was won from Europe, not given by it.

5. Today. China and Russia invoke 'Westphalian' non-interference, and Acharya describes a multiplex order. Non-Western actors now shape the order's direction.

Conclusion: European power was decisive in the 19th century. But the modern order is better seen as the product of global interaction, in which non-European agency both preceded European dominance and later dismantled its imperial form.

questions.q: Which IR theory best explains challenges to the dominant international order in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries? Answer with reference to at least one twentieth-century and one twenty-first-century challenger.
markScheme: Sets out clear criteria for 'best explains' (explanatory scope, timing, actors' motives)
Accurate statement of realism (Waltz, Mearsheimer, power transition), liberal internationalism (Keohane, Doyle, Ikenberry) and constructivism (Wendt, Ruggie, Mitzen)
20th-century case analysed accurately: e.g. Japan (1919 Racial Equality Proposal, 1922 naval ratio, 1931–41) or Germany (Tooze on the US benchmark)
21st-century case analysed accurately: e.g. Russia (2007 Munich, 2014 Crimea, 2022 invasion) or China (BRI, global initiatives)
Weighs material power shifts against status, recognition and identity; uses Barnhart, Shimazu or Larson and Shevchenko where relevant
Considers liberal accounts (institutions and interdependence restraining or failing to restrain challengers)
Reaches a reasoned judgement, possibly a synthesis, rather than a list
Current events stated accurately as of 2026
questions.modelAnswer:
Thesis: Realism best explains when challenges arise, since they track shifts in relative power. Constructivist attention to status and recognition best explains why challengers act as they do and how they choose targets. The strongest account combines the two, and liberalism explains mainly the limits of challenge.

Realism. For Waltz, anarchy produces balancing. For Mearsheimer and power-transition theorists (Organski, Allison), rising states try to revise orders that reflect older distributions of power. Interwar Japan fits. Industrialised after 1868 and victorious over Russia (1904–05), it outgrew an order fixed by Britain and the US, symbolised by the 5:5:3 ratio of 1922, and expanded when it could (Manchuria 1931, China 1937). Tooze shows that Hitler measured Germany against American power. Today China's growth and naval build-up fit the same logic.

Constructivism. Realism struggles with motives and choices. Shimazu shows that Japan's 1919 Racial Equality Proposal was about recognition as an equal great power, and its rejection fed a sense of humiliation. Barnhart shows that humiliated states seek status through territory. Russia since Putin's Munich speech (2007) frames its grievances in terms of respect and spheres of influence (Larson and Shevchenko). Its annexations of Crimea (2014) and Ukrainian regions (2022) are hard to explain in narrow power terms alone, given the sanctions and costs. Mitzen's ontological security helps explain persistence in costly confrontation.

Liberalism. Keohane and Ikenberry predict that institutions and interdependence make challenge costly and integration attractive. China's rise largely within the WTO since 2001 offers partial support. But interdependence did not deter Russia in 2022, and Farrell and Newman show that interdependence can itself be weaponised.

Judgement. Realism identifies the conditions for challenge, a shifting balance of power. Constructivism explains its form and intensity, especially status grievances. Russia, often described as a declining power, challenging violently while the war remains unresolved in late 2026, is hard for pure power-transition theory but easy for a status-based account. The best explanation is therefore a realist-constructivist synthesis, with liberalism explaining why some rising states, such as China so far, mostly pursue revision through economic and institutional means rather than conquest.
